title: Birds: Anatomy, Behavior, and Field Identification
description: An introduction to the biology of birds for learners with no formal background. The course moves from what makes a bird a bird (feathers, skeleton and evolutionary history) through flight, internal anatomy and the senses, to the practical skill of identifying birds by sight and sound. Later chapters cover breeding, migration and the conservation of bird populations. Each chapter pairs reading with practice you can do outdoors or with photographs and recordings.
objectives: Describe the anatomical traits that define birds and explain how they support flight.
Explain the evidence that birds are living dinosaurs.
Identify common birds to species using shape, field marks, behavior, habitat and sound.
Describe how birds court, nest, raise young and migrate.
Interpret bird population data and explain the main threats to birds and the measures that have reversed declines.
Collect and submit a standardized bird survey to a citizen-science project.

preface:
This book is an introduction to the biology of birds for readers who have never studied it formally. It begins with the question that defines the field, what makes a bird a bird, and answers it with anatomy and the fossil record before turning to flight, physiology, identification, song, breeding, migration and conservation. Each chapter rests on the ones before it, so the order matters.

Every section follows the same plan. Read the text, study the figure, work through the example, then attempt the three practice problems before moving on. The chapter quiz checks whether the ideas have settled; the challenge exercises ask you to use them on real birds. Numbers in square brackets point to the sources listed after each section. I have kept to the scholarly literature and standard references so that you can follow any claim back to its evidence.

Ornithology rewards patience and attention more than prior knowledge. A notebook, a field guide and an hour outdoors each week will teach you as much as these pages, and the two together will teach you more than either alone.

title: Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience
description: A course for learners who have played games critically and perhaps made small prototypes, and now want the working methods of professional designers. It treats a game as a system of rules that produces player experience, and teaches the tools designers use to shape that system: core loops, feedback, economies, difficulty curves, level layout and playtesting. Every chapter ends with a design exercise that you can complete on paper or in a simple prototype.

Basic arithmetic and spreadsheets; no programming required

preface:
I wrote this book for people who have played a lot of games, maybe built a prototype or two, and now want to work the way designers in studios work. It is a working manual more than a theory text. Each chapter hands you one set of tools (core loops, feedback, economies, difficulty curves, level layout, playtesting) and then asks you to use them on a real design.

Do the exercises. You can read about a dominant strategy in five minutes; you learn to spot one by breaking your own card game on a Tuesday night. Paper, index cards and a spreadsheet are all you need for every challenge here, and paper prototypes will teach you faster than code because you can change a rule in ten seconds.

Expect your first designs to be bad. Everyone's are. The skill this book is really about is noticing why a design is not working and changing it, which is why the chapter on playtesting matters more than any other.

Distances and sizes are built up with everyday comparisons before any numbers are introduced. You will finish able to find major objects in the night sky and explain how astronomers know what they know.

preface:
Hello. This book is about space, and it starts right where you are standing. You do not need to know anything yet. You only need to look up.

We will start with things you can see with your own eyes: the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars. Then we will go a little farther in each chapter, past the planets, out to other stars, and all the way to other galaxies. Each part is short. Read it, look at the pictures, and try the little questions at the end. If a question is hard, that is fine. Go back and read it again.

Some numbers in space are very big. When they are, I will compare them to things you know, like a walk to the store or a grain of sand. Every fact in this book is true and checked, even when the words are simple.

title: Energy Systems: Conversion, Storage, and the Electric Grid
department: Department of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering
description: An upper-division treatment of how societies convert, store, move and use energy. The course applies thermodynamics, electrical engineering and economics to real systems: thermal power plants, wind and solar generation, batteries and other storage, and the operation of the power grid. Students work with quantitative models throughout, including efficiency limits, capacity factors, levelized cost and dispatch. The final chapter combines these tools to evaluate decarbonization pathways.

preface:
Every energy system is a chain of conversions, and every link in the chain loses something. This book traces those chains with numbers: from fuel, wind or sunlight, through engines, turbines and semiconductors, onto a grid that must match supply to demand second by second, and into the motors, lights and heat pumps where energy finally does useful work.

The tools are thermodynamics, circuit theory and a little economics. If you are comfortable with calculus and introductory physics, you have what you need; the first chapters rebuild the rest. Expect to compute: Carnot limits, line losses, capacity factors, levelized costs. Build the habit of order-of-magnitude reasoning, because most bad energy arguments fail at the first multiplication.

The last chapter puts the pieces together on the question that now drives the field: how to run an electric system with far less carbon. You will finish able to read a decarbonization study and say which of its assumptions matter.
